name: Olga Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Olga, 43, and I run a drilling rig at the large mine. I have a vocational certificate and enough years here to hear when a bit is wearing out, but I still earn toward the low end of the crew scale. My partner repairs bicycles, so his weekly takings change, and our two school-age children and mortgage leave us with less than a month's expenses saved. There aren't many mines within reach of our house, and I don't use AI tools; I rely on the logbook and the people on the shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that routine software won't fix our short staffing. Our union should keep pressing for predictable rosters and fair pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mortgage is tight even if AI mostly fizzles. One missed weekend shift can use up the small amount we have saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the drill rig and recording bit wear in the paper log. I'd attend the next union meeting about weekend rosters and base pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious already, because a quiet technology story doesn't make our household income steady. My partner can have a poor repair week just as I lose an overtime shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill worries you after a short week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage is the first fixed payment, and then there's the children's school transport. Last month I moved the grocery list around after a cancelled Saturday shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep a paper log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can hand a page to the next operator and show exactly when the vibration changed. I know the mine has screens, but I haven't seen a reason to replace the record I trust.

Our **union** should keep pressing for predictable rosters and fair pay.
think: My **mortgage** is tight even if AI mostly fizzles.
One missed weekend **shift** can use up the small amount we have saved.
do: Keep running the **drill rig** and recording bit wear in the paper log.
Attend the next **union meeting** about weekend rosters and base pay.
feel: **Anxious** about existing unstable overtime and thin savings.
S0.quote: Last month I moved the grocery list around after a cancelled Saturday shift.
fieldNote: Her **thin cushion** and variable household earnings make the mild scenario financially tense before any major AI shift.
She values the familiar **paper log** and sees collective bargaining over rosters as more urgent than changing tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planners need a voice when software takes over checking and schedules. The crew must be told when a new roster cuts paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My rig still needs an operator, but automated planning could reduce the overtime I depend on. If dispatch loses staff, I worry about rushed drill instructions reaching us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the shift representative for a roster comparison before the software starts. I'd cut our monthly takeaway meals if overtime falls this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious because the card leaves hands-on work for longer but moves the schedules that decide my pay. I don't have the spare money to wait calmly through a bad trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the representative to compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want last winter's paid hours beside the first software roster, including the weekend calls. A tidy average can hide the two shifts that pay for our heating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the planning tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the mine showed me at work and paid for that time, perhaps. I won't borrow money for a course in a system that might only reduce my hours.

feel: **Anxious** that planning changes could remove needed overtime.
S1.quote: A tidy average can hide the two shifts that pay for our heating.
fieldNote: Her **hands-on role** lasts longer than planning jobs, but an automated roster can still shrink her near-term income.
She wants the **union** to compare actual paid hours and would cut a small household expense if those hours fall.

steps.text: Ask shift representative to compare paid hours before and after software rosters
Cut monthly takeaway meals if winter overtime drops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew 2028 AGI may change the office before the drilling face. By 2031, robots could take our rig shifts, and workers need income protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45 in 2028, my drilling may continue, but the people writing work orders could go. At 48 in 2031, I expect the mine to replace most rigs with robots and my wage to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union's robot transition committee this month to demand paid placement support. I'd apply for municipal equipment openings as soon as robot orders are announced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed; I lie awake counting what we owe because the mine wage could disappear while the children are still at home. Less than a month of savings would vanish before we found another local job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm looking at other equipment jobs and that they should keep doing their schoolwork. I wouldn't tell them the mortgage arithmetic that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for another mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after looking at every local opening and talking to my partner. Moving two children in the middle of school for a job that robots might also take would be a hard gamble.

By **2031**, robots could take our rig shifts, and workers need income protection.
think: At 45 in **2028**, my drilling may continue, but the people writing work orders could go.
At 48 in **2031**, I expect the mine to replace most rigs with robots and my wage to go.
do: Join the union's **robot transition committee** this month to demand paid placement support.
Apply for **municipal equipment** openings as soon as robot orders are announced.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected wage loss and nights spent counting debts.
S2.quote: Less than a month of savings would vanish before we found another local job.
fieldNote: She expects a **2031 rig replacement** and describes sleepless calculation against a mortgage and almost no savings.
She prefers **union placement** demands and local equipment applications before risking a school move for another exposed mine job.

steps.text: Join union robot transition committee this month to seek paid placement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd demand a 2034 rig plan before the mine starts replacing operators. Five years before AGI is enough to negotiate paid retraining if management sits down now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031, AI might rewrite work orders while I still drill. At 51 in 2034, our children will be older, but the mortgage and my need for work will remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our union representative to seek paid training in waterworks machinery this year. I'd enroll in that waterworks course if the mine funds fees and work hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but five years gives me a chance to argue for a real path rather than just a payout. I can't pay for classes myself while the mortgage takes most of a low mine wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why waterworks machinery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The local water utility has a maintenance yard, and I've worked with pumps as well as the drill. I don't know whether they'll hire me, but it's a place I could reach without moving the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid training place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, an unpaid place would push us behind on the house. I'd ask the union to make paid release time part of any agreement, not just a free course leaflet.

say: I'd demand a **2034 rig plan** before the mine starts replacing operators.
Five years before AGI is enough to negotiate **paid retraining** if management sits down now.
think: At 48 in **2031**, AI might rewrite work orders while I still drill.
At 51 in **2034**, our children will be older, but the mortgage and my need for work will remain.
do: Ask our union representative to seek **paid training** in waterworks machinery this year.
Enroll in that **waterworks course** if the mine funds fees and work hours.
feel: **Anxious** about cost, with time to seek funded training.
S3.quote: I'd ask the union to make paid release time part of any agreement, not just a free course leaflet.
fieldNote: The **2034 robot date** offers more bargaining time, yet she cannot self-fund training with a thin cushion.
Her interest in nearby **waterworks** follows existing pump experience and a desire to keep the family in its home.

steps.text: Ask union representative to negotiate paid waterworks machinery training this year
Enroll in waterworks course if mine covers fees and work hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a 2039 deadline should come with written training rights. The mine shouldn't wait until a robot order to tell families what happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, AI may handle records while I still operate the rig. At 56 in 2039, I could still need wages, even if our children are grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the drill shifts while the mine still pays operators. I'd press the union each year for a written training and placement agreement before 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about money now, not just about a robot thirteen years away. The longer warning makes the job change less sudden, but it doesn't give us a month's savings by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would retirement solve the 2039 problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't put retirement on a calendar because the children grow up. We'll still have ordinary bills, and I don't know what the mortgage balance will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might you do with a good year of shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the extra pay into an emergency account, starting with one full month of expenses. That would let us say yes to a course or a job interview without fearing the next bill.

say: I'd tell the crew a **2039 deadline** should come with written training rights.
The mine shouldn't wait until a **robot order** to tell families what happens.
think: At 53 in **2036**, AI may handle records while I still operate the rig.
At 56 in **2039**, I could still need wages, even if our children are grown.
do: Keep the **drill shifts** while the mine still pays operators.
Press the union each year for a written **training and placement agreement** before 2039.
feel: **Anxious** about today's thin reserve despite a long warning.
S4.quote: The longer warning makes the job change less sudden, but it doesn't give us a month's savings by itself.
fieldNote: Her **current income pressure** keeps her anxious even when robots are thirteen years away.
She would keep **paid drilling** work, bargain for written placement rights and use any extra shifts to build one month of reserves.

steps.text: Keep paid drill shifts while the mine employs operators
Press union annually for written training and placement rights
Save extra shift pay until the emergency account holds one month of expenses

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because a 2031 robot fleet could take my wage before we have savings or another job nearby. Paid training and a written right to placement would help, along with notice of actual rig orders.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who pays the mortgage while a worker trains. A course without wages attached is a piece of paper I can't use.

headlineQuote: A course without wages attached is a piece of paper I can't use.
portrait: Olga is a **43-year-old** experienced drill operator with a vocational certificate and pay near the low end of the crew scale.
Her partner's bicycle repairs vary by week, and two school-age children, a **mortgage** and thin savings press on the household.
She trusts familiar **paper records**, avoids new AI tools and uses the union to seek predictable hours and enforceable rights.
The **2031 robot threat** alarms her; longer warnings let her bargain for paid training, although today's money remains tight.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because robots could remove her wage in 2031 with little savings or local work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training**, placement rights and notice of rig orders would let her seek another reachable job while meeting the mortgage.
